topline: Three stories today: a gunman kills six on Kraków's main square in what Polish officials call terrorism, EU prosecutors open a second fraud probe into funds for Spain's crash-hit Madrid–Seville rail line three weeks before a snap election, and France sees a fourth weekend of cost-of-living protests.

stories.title: Gunman kills six on Kraków's Main Market Square; Poland declares national mourning
stories.summary: A 24-year-old Polish man drove onto Kraków's Main Market Square on Saturday afternoon and fired a military-style rifle at passers-by, killing six people (four women and two men) and wounding around 15, including two police officers. Police shot and detained him; officials say he acted alone, and further firearms and ammunition were found in his car. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said early indications were that the suspect was drawn to far-right ideas, though police had not formally established a motive. Prime Minister Donald Tusk praised the police response and urged against speculation, President Karol Nawrocki called for a full explanation and declared national mourning, and EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz sent condolences. Some reports say three more bodies were later found at the suspect's family home.
stories.why: It is one of the deadliest attacks in an EU member state this year and lands in a deeply polarised Poland, where government and president are already at odds; how the motive is framed will shape debates on gun licensing and political extremism across the bloc.

left.angle: Left-leaning and international outlets led with the death toll, the police response and the wave of solidarity from EU and foreign leaders, treating the motive as still unclear. They placed the attack in the context of rarely seen gun violence in Poland and earlier violent incidents, with little focus on domestic political fallout.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Wire-based account stressing the toll, Tusk's praise for police and Kallas's condolences; no motive discussed.

outlets.name: taz
outlets.note: Cautious on motive; focuses on eyewitnesses sheltering in shops and questions about police presence that day.

right.angle: Conservative coverage put the interior minister's 'far-right' remark in the headline but quickly stressed that police had not confirmed any ideology, and dug into the suspect's background, weapons licence and family. It gave more room to the terror label used by ministers and to Nawrocki's demand for a full investigation than to international reactions.

outlets.name: Hungarian Conservative
outlets.note: Leads with the minister's claim, notes it is unconfirmed, and reports the bodies found at the family home and the father's gun collection.

stories.differ: Left-leaning reports emphasised grief, solidarity and caution about motive; the conservative piece focused on the suspect's profile and questioned how firmly the government could yet label him far-right.

stories.title: EU prosecutors open a second fraud probe into funds for Spain's crash-hit Madrid–Seville rail line
stories.summary: The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) has opened, on its own initiative, an investigation into possible fraud involving EU money for renovating the Madrid–Seville high-speed line, where a crash near Urda on 28 October killed 69 people. The line received €111 million in EU regional development funding in 2024; the Guardia Civil's UCO unit collected documents from rail operator Adif, the state rail safety agency and the Court of Auditors on EPPO's behalf. It is the second EPPO probe on the line after a January crash at Adamuz killed 46. Transport Minister Óscar Puente resigned on 3 November, and the affair is unfolding ahead of Spain's snap general election on 29 November.
stories.why: It tests the EPPO's role in policing how member states spend EU recovery and cohesion money, and could sway a national election in one of the bloc's largest economies.

left.angle: Left-leaning coverage treated the probe as a matter of infrastructure and EU oversight: what the EPPO is examining, how it relates to the earlier Adamuz case, and the Commission's own past warnings that the 1992 line was outdated. It kept the judicial track separate from the election campaign.

outlets.name: elDiario.es
outlets.note: Brussels correspondent's report on the EPPO and UCO steps, stressing the line's age and the separate judicial inquiry into the crash.

right.angle: Right-leaning coverage linked the probe to Adif's management and to the Sánchez government, highlighting a large signalling contract signed with EU recovery funds and audit-office concerns over who signed it. It framed the investigations as a blow to the Socialists' campaign, while one report itself noted the auditors did not find the signatures false.

outlets.name: The Objective
outlets.note: Focuses on a €77.5 million signalling contract and Court of Auditors doubts over the signatories' powers.

outlets.name: The Objective
outlets.note: Argues the Adif probes are damaging Sánchez's 29 November campaign, citing anonymous Socialist figures.

stories.differ: The left treats the probe as an oversight question about ageing infrastructure and EU money; the right treats it as evidence of mismanagement under Sánchez with direct electoral consequences.

stories.title: France holds a fourth weekend of cost-of-living protests as official turnout falls
stories.summary: Protests against the rising cost of living took place across France on Saturday for the fourth weekend running. The Interior Ministry counted about 146,000 demonstrators nationwide, 46,000 of them in Paris, while organisers claimed 250,000; official figures have fallen each week from about 550,000 in mid-October. Some 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed, police used tear gas in Paris and Lyon, and early counts reported 18 arrests. The movement, which began with student protests over school conditions, now combines youth groups, union branches and a separate 'yellow vests' rally.
stories.why: Sustained unrest in the eurozone's second-largest economy feeds into France's budget choices and a presidential race due in April, in which polls show the National Rally ahead.

left.angle: Left-leaning coverage stressed the size and breadth of the movement, the clashes and the interior minister's warning to rioters, and tied the protests to the coming presidential race. Its emphasis was on public anger rather than on falling numbers.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Leads with 140,000-plus marchers and tear gas, and notes Le Pen and Mélenchon leading the polls.

right.angle: We could not find a right-leaning outlet's take on Saturday's protests in time for this edition. Straight-news and business-oriented reports instead stressed the steady fall in official turnout and calmer marches.

stories.differ: The available coverage splits between protests that remain large and angry and a movement that is losing steam; no right-leaning framing could be verified today.
